topStories.headline: Super El Niño Storm Swamps the Mission, Leaves Restaurants and Residents Reeling
topStories.dek: An atmospheric river broke a 108-year rainfall record on November 18, flooding streets, garages, and businesses across the Mission District — and sending raw sewage up through floor drains.
topStories.body:
A powerful storm swept San Francisco on Wednesday, November 18, dropping 2.28 inches of rain in a single day — a record for that date going back to 1918, according to the San Francisco Chronicle. In the Mission District, Folsom Street between 14th and 18th Streets was transformed into a lake, with water pooling several feet deep at the worst points and manhole covers floating loose in flooded intersections.

The damage hit hardest in low-lying blocks built over historic creek beds. Businesses including Pink Onion Pizza, Rainbow Grocery, and Bageletto — a bagel shop that had opened less than two years ago — were all forced to close Thursday for cleanup. The flooding at many sites came not from the street but from below: sewage surged up through toilets, sinks, and floor drains, overwhelming even the floodgates that some owners had installed at significant cost. Bageletto owner Rich D'Aloia told CBS San Francisco that his shop ended up under about a foot of contaminated water, destroying thousands of dollars of food and equipment.

A dialysis center in the Mission also had to cancel kidney treatments after its ground floor flooded, according to a 311 complaint reviewed by the SF Standard. Mayor Daniel Lurie visited affected businesses on Thursday and acknowledged the damage. He told Mission Local he is working with the Board of Supervisors to determine whether compensation for flood-damaged businesses is possible, though no commitment has been made.

Residents and business owners said they want the city to explain how flooding this severe happened — and to present a plan before the next wave of El Niño storms arrives. The National Weather Service had warned that more rain is expected over the coming week.

topStories.headline: SFUSD Can't Produce Basic Records on Bernal Preschool It Plans to Shut Down
topStories.dek: The district quietly notified parents in September that Junipero Serra Annex Early Education School in Bernal Heights will close in July 2027 — but it has yet to provide the school's official enrollment code or explain how the decision was made.
topStories.body:
San Francisco Unified School District notified parents at Junipero Serra Annex Early Education School in mid-September that the Bernal Heights site would close in July 2027 and their roughly 80 preschool and transitional kindergarten students would be reassigned to two other district campuses. Parents say they were blindsided, having received the news just weeks into the school year.

Mission Local reported this week that the district has been unable — or unwilling — to produce its own internal records about the school. After repeated requests beginning November 10, SFUSD had not provided the school's California Data System code, which is needed to look up its official enrollment figures online. The district's spokesperson asked for more time.

The dispute matters because how the Annex is officially classified determines what procedural rights parents have. If the Annex is treated as an independent school, the closure would trigger a lengthy public process including board hearings. SFUSD School Board President Phil Kim has said the board need not vote on the closure because the Annex is simply an extension of the adjacent Junipero Serra Elementary School. Parents disagree, noting that the two schools operate separately at different addresses.

The school is located at 155 Appleton Avenue, a stone's throw from Holly Park. The district held only one community meeting — on October 29, more than 40 days after parents first received the closure notice, according to Mission Local.

topStories.headline: A Shuttered Mission Walgreens Will Finally Become a Child Care Center for SF General Workers
topStories.dek: After nearly 40 years of advocacy by hospital employees and their union, the city has begun permitting a child care facility at 1189 Potrero Avenue — the former Walgreens that closed in early 2025.
topStories.body:
The vacant Walgreens storefront at 1189 Potrero Avenue, at the corner of 24th Street, is set to become a child care center for employees of Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital — a goal that nurses and hospital workers have been fighting for since the late 1980s. Mission Local reported the development on November 18.

The facility will serve up to 53 infants, toddlers, and preschoolers up to age 5. Priority will go to hospital employees and other city workers, with neighborhood families also eligible. The city agreed in principle to build a child care center for hospital employees as far back as 1993, and again in 2007 as part of a union contract. A new seven-story hospital building was completed in 2016 without one. The permitting process for the conversion finally began in August 2026, according to SFist.

The Walgreens at that address closed in February 2025. It had been the only full-service pharmacy within walking distance of the hospital, and its closure drew criticism from community members and local elected officials. The building now has a new purpose — though permitting and construction mean the child care center is still some time away from opening.

moreNews.headline: Mission Branch Library Reopens After Six-Year Closure
moreNews.body: San Francisco's Mission Branch Library at 3359 24th Street reopened to the public on Saturday, November 14, with a free grand reopening celebration from noon to 1 p.m. The landmark building — one of seven city libraries designated as San Francisco landmarks — had been closed for a lengthy renovation. The reopening had been delayed multiple times, most recently in May 2026, before the doors finally opened last weekend.

moreNews.headline: Radio Habana to Add Daytime Cafe at Its Valencia Street Space
moreNews.body: Radio Habana Social Club, the long-running Cuban bar and community gathering spot at 1109 Valencia Street, announced in its November 11 Mission Buzz column that it will begin operating as a coffee shop during daytime hours starting later this month. Regulars Aziz Saeed and Sarah Zeidat will manage the new Radio Habana Cafe, sharing the space with the existing evening bar operation. The venue has been a Mission District fixture since 1998.
